subject: physics
question_text: What are collisions? Explain the possible types of collisions. Develop the theory of one-dimensional elastic collision.

verification.note: Sri Chaitanya IPE Junior Fastrack (Rev. May 2024), Unit 6 LONG ANSWER 3, and the TSBIE Basic Learning Material carries the same question in its Unit 6 Long Answer set. The Fastrack ALSO asks the relative-velocity result alone as SHORT ANSWER 1, which is why this file carries two cuts rather than two answers. Both splits are invented and need a Telangana IPE teacher; no exam appearance years are printed, so appearances[] stays empty.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: What a collision is
lines: A collision is a strong interaction
between two bodies in which momentum is
exchanged in a very short time.
Example: two billiard balls striking.
steps.margin_note: The words worth the mark are "short time" — that is what separates a collision from an ordinary push.
steps.why: Because the interaction is brief, outside forces have almost no time to act, which is exactly why momentum can be treated as conserved.
common_mistakes: Defining a collision as bodies touching. Two charged particles can collide without ever touching.

recall.must_convey: That a collision is a strong, short-lived interaction in which momentum is exchanged.
accept: momentum is exchanged in a short time

steps.memory_tip: Two words carry the definition: a SHORT, STRONG interaction — too short for outside forces to matter.

steps.label: The two types
lines: both the momentum and the kinetic
energy of the system are conserved.
Example: collisions between atomic and
subatomic particles.
only the momentum is conserved; the
kinetic energy is not.
Example: a ball struck by a bat.
steps.margin_note: Each type gets a definition AND an example. The example is a separate thing to lose.
steps.why: Momentum survives both kinds because the forces are internal. Kinetic energy only survives when nothing is left behind as heat, sound or a dent.
common_mistakes: Saying momentum is not conserved in an inelastic collision. It always is.

recall.must_convey: That elastic conserves both momentum and kinetic energy, inelastic conserves only momentum, with an example of each.
accept: atomic particles and a ball hit by a bat

steps.memory_tip: One sentence each: both types conserve momentum; only the elastic one also conserves kinetic energy.

steps.label: The set-up
steps.margin_note: Three panels — before, during, after — with every velocity named. The whole derivation reads off this picture.
steps.why: Six symbols appear in the algebra. The figure is where each one is attached to a body, which is what stops the signs going wrong.
common_mistakes: Drawing only "before" and "after", losing the contact moment where the forces act.

recall.must_convey: That a before / during / after figure is drawn with the masses and all four velocities labelled.
accept: figure with m1 m2 u1 u2 v1 v2

steps.memory_tip: Draw the two balls twice — before with u₁, u₂ and after with v₁, v₂ — so every symbol sits on a body.

steps.label: Momentum equation
lines: Two bodies of masses m₁ and m₂ move
along the same line with velocities u₁
and u₂ (u₁ > u₂). After the collision
their velocities are v₁ and v₂.
By conservation of linear momentum,
steps.margin_note: Introduce all six symbols here, then write the equation. Number it — the next steps refer back to it.
steps.why: Rearranging into (1) groups each body with its own change of velocity, which is what makes the division two steps later cancel so cleanly.
common_mistakes: Not numbering the equations, then having nothing to name when dividing them.

recall.must_convey: That conservation of momentum gives m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂, rearranged as equation (1).
accept: m1 u1 plus m2 u2 equals m1 v1 plus m2 v2

steps.memory_tip: Equation (1): group each mass with its own velocity change: m₁(u₁ − v₁) = m₂(v₂ − u₂).

steps.label: Energy equation
lines: The collision is elastic, so the total
kinetic energy is also conserved:
steps.margin_note: Say "elastic" out loud before using this. It is the only reason the equation is allowed.
steps.why: This is the step that is false for an inelastic collision, which is why the whole result belongs to elastic collisions alone.
common_mistakes: Using the kinetic-energy equation without stating that the collision is elastic.

recall.must_convey: That because the collision is elastic, kinetic energy is also conserved, giving equation (2).
accept: half m1 u1 squared plus half m2 u2 squared

steps.memory_tip: Equation (2) is the elastic-only line: the same grouping, with squares.

steps.label: Relative velocities
lines: Dividing (2) by (1),
The relative velocity of approach before
the collision equals the relative
velocity of separation after it.
steps.margin_note: Finish with the sentence in words. The examiner is looking for that statement, not only the algebra.
steps.why: Dividing is only allowed because the bodies actually collide and separate, so u₁ ≠ v₁ and the factors being cancelled are not zero. The book never says this, but a division by zero is what it would otherwise be.
common_mistakes: Writing u₁ − u₂ = v₁ − v₂, with the two final velocities the wrong way round.

recall.must_convey: That dividing (2) by (1) gives u₁ − u₂ = v₂ − v₁: approach speed equals separation speed.
accept: u1 minus u2 equals v2 minus v1
relative velocity of approach equals relative velocity of separation

steps.memory_tip: Divide (2) by (1): speed of approach = speed of separation.

steps.label: The final velocities
lines: Substituting (3) into (1) and solving,
and writing D = m₁ + m₂,
steps.margin_note: Writing D = m₁ + m₂ once keeps both lines on one rule. Say what D stands for.
steps.why: Check them against a case you know: with equal masses, m₁ − m₂ = 0 and the two bodies simply swap velocities — which is what happens on a carrom board.
common_mistakes: Swapping the u₁ and u₂ terms between the two expressions.

recall.must_convey: That the final velocities are v₁ and v₂ in terms of the masses and initial velocities over m₁ + m₂.
accept: v1 equals m1 minus m2 into u1 plus two m2 u2 by the sum
v2 has two m1 u1 in it
reject: u1 minus u2 equals v2 minus v1

steps.memory_tip: Check the result with equal masses: the two velocities simply swap.

cuts.label: 4-mark answer
cuts.question_text: Show that in the case of a one-dimensional elastic collision, the relative velocity of approach of the two colliding bodies before collision is equal to the relative velocity of separation after collision.

s6_divide.label: The result
s6_divide.margin_note: This is what the question asks for. Finish with the sentence in words, not only the algebra.

insider_note: The division step, equation (2) by equation (1), is where most students stop — practise that one line.
